chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
title: Night Train, French waltzes and renewing the crowd
summary: Butler used Night Train, which Crouch says derives from Ellington's Deep South Suite, plus French songs and the Merry Widow waltz to turn the room.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So then, I'm not going to get up there, that comparison. I got up there and jumped into "Night Train" again. (Humming). Started putting that Kansas City stuff away. (Simultaneous conversation.)
Well, now, you know that's Duke Ellington's tune.
That comes out of a piece he called "Deep South Suite." And there's a train portion of it, (humming).
Okay, also now, Mingus one on it (humming). Then he repeats, and then he's got a bridge that he puts on it. But, you know, Ellington wrote that, it wasn't Jimmy Forrest.

So, I moved that, when I got in trouble, I put that on him, or anybody. Then I had an old waltz written, "Ballet de Picalle." And then I go into the French stuff, see. I'd go on and play French numbers and (French.)

You can never understand how much I love you. (French). (Singing). So you've got to know how to do it. Now, written in the romantic mood, then you pop out there, sometimes I'd pop out there and (inaudible). Play the "Merry Widow Waltz" (humming). They would be gone. That speed was there. And that's how I renewed it.
